### EvalApp: a self-tuning async pipeline runtime for .NET

Run everything at once without overloading anything. Gates on every resource, sagas that undo failures, and a tuner that finds the right speed.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp, release 4.4.2: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp.Neural, release 2.0.3: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp.Neural`
- Used by: HoloDb, AlgFormer, Prose, Tracer
- Tools: Doctrine

Run it all at once without overloading anything.

Describe a process as plain steps. EvalApp gates every database, disk and network call at a bound you set, undoes failed work in reverse order, and can tune the bound for you. No broker, no services to stand up.

- 7 of 7: recorded runs where the most downloads in flight equalled the gate bound
- 1,113 ms to 139 ms: time to finish 24 jobs at a bound of 1 and at the best bound, 8
- 2.9 times: slower with all 24 jobs running at once than at the best bound

EvalApp replaces the plumbing that every real async .NET codebase ends up writing by hand: a SemaphoreSlim to stop a flood of requests hammering a database, a guessed constant for how many things run at once, a Task.WhenAll inside a try and catch to collect failures, and a rollback path bolted on after something breaks halfway through.

You describe a process as a plain data record and a sequence of steps. EvalApp compiles that into one reusable execution path and gates every resource it touches (CPU, network, disk, database or a pool of your own) at a real bound. When you turn tuning on, it looks for the concurrency that works on the hardware it runs on, instead of a number someone picked once. It is the runtime under the other Evaluated Applications libraries, and it works on its own: no broker, no external service, no config store.

Why use it:
- One dependency instead of a stack. Where you would reach for a DI container, MediatR, Polly and TPL Dataflow, EvalApp is a single compiled pipeline that covers fan-out, resource gating, fallback steps and compensation together.
- The tuner probes, it does not wait for a failure. A circuit breaker waits for something to break and then responds. The adaptive tuner keeps probing for the operating point that stops things breaking, independently for each instance and with no coordination. A Bayesian mode keeps what it learned across restarts.
- Whole categories of coordination bugs do not compile. A saga you open has to be closed before the pipeline builds. A step with a side effect cannot be added without declaring the resource it touches, so there is no way to write an ungated side effect.
- The builder chain is the architecture. Read the fluent declaration from top to bottom and it reads like the process it describes. It is the code, not documentation about the code, so it cannot drift out of date the way a diagram does.
- Nothing to stand up first. It is a package reference, not infrastructure. Most pipeline libraries want a broker or a database before the first item is processed. EvalApp does not.

Capabilities:
- Fluent pipeline builder. Eval.App(...) leads to domains, tasks and steps, compiled once into an immutable, reusable ICompiledPipeline<T>.
- Resource-gated concurrency. Declare Network, DiskIO, Cpu, Database or a named pool of your own, and every step that touches it contends for the same bound.
- Adaptive and Bayesian tuning. A hill-climbing tuner that rediscovers the optimum on each run, or a Bayesian tuner whose performance model survives restarts. Both are opt-in and stay inside the bounds you declare.
- Parallel ForEach and parallel branches. Bounded per-item fan-out over a collection, where Tunable.ForItems() lets the tuner pick the count, and a fixed set of concurrent branches with configurable merge strategies.
- Sagas with compensation. Chain steps with an undo. When a later step fails, every earlier compensation runs in reverse order.
- Middleware. Wrap any step for retry, timing or audit by implementing IStepMiddleware<T>. It is a seam you implement, not a library of ready-made ones.
- Pipelines that run pipelines. A compiled pipeline is a value. A step can run another pipeline or itself, so an outer schedule loop can drive an inner per-batch pipeline, or a pipeline can recurse through a tree, with no orchestration code of your own. PipelineRef<T> forward-declares a pipeline, PipelineTrace tells same-named steps apart across levels, and runaway recursion fails cleanly instead of overflowing the stack.
- A harness for things that are not thread-safe. Declare an ExclusiveResource once (a GPU context, a native handle, a single-writer file), guard a scope or named branches with it, and a second concurrent entry fails loudly or queues, as you choose. It is re-entrant for recursion, and forks inside a held scope exclude each other.
- Single-thread hosts. In a browser, on a one-core process or when you say so, EvalApp detects it once and stops fanning out. ForEach, parallel groups and ChunkedWork run inline, and long runs hand the thread back every few milliseconds so a page stays responsive. On a multi-core host none of it is active.
- Results as data. PipelineResult<T> is Success, Failure or Skipped, matched with a switch instead of caught.
- Offline licence check. The licence validator every Evaluated Applications package embeds is part of the package. It runs entirely offline with ECDsa P-256 and makes no network call.

Quick start:

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Orders")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep("Validate", d =>
            {
                if (d.Total <= 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Total must be positive");
                return d with { Status = "Validated" };
            })
            .AddStep("ApplyDiscount", d => d with { Total = d.Total * 0.9m })
            .AddStep("Complete", d => d with { Status = "Complete" })
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

// Build once, at startup. Run as many times as you like.
var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 99.99m));

switch (result)
{
    case PipelineResult<OrderData>.Success success:
        Console.WriteLine($"{success.Data.Status}: {success.Data.Total}");
        break;
    case PipelineResult<OrderData>.Failure failure:
        Console.WriteLine($"Failed: {failure.Exception.Message}");
        break;
    case PipelineResult<OrderData>.Skipped skipped:
        Console.WriteLine($"Skipped: {skipped.Reason}");
        break;
}

// Top-level statements come first, so the record goes last.
public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");
```

Output:

```text
Complete: 89.991
```

Limits:
- Work that has to survive a process restart over hours or days belongs to a workflow engine such as Temporal. EvalApp runs in process.
- Purely reactive resilience, which detects a break and responds to it, is what Polly is for. EvalApp is for the case in between: no infrastructure to stand up, throughput that matters and concurrency that tunes itself.
- ICompiledPipeline<T> is opaque. It exposes a name and RunAsync. Report() gives a read-only view of the plan, with call counts for each ForEach node.
- The builder and step-construction path is safe to trim and to compile ahead of time. The tuner's file persistence and a couple of internal caches still use reflection-based JSON and raise trimmer warnings under PublishTrimmed, so leave WithTuning off if that matters for your build.
- The package ships as a binary with no source and no XML documentation. Author against the root EvalApp namespace; everything public lives there.

#### EvalApp docs (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp/docs/)

A practical guide to building with EvalApp. Describe a process as a typed data record and a sequence of steps, gate every resource it touches, and let tuning find the concurrency that suits the hardware. Every program on this page is compiled and run against the published package.

##### Install

Add the package with dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp. It targets net8.0 and net10.0 and has no dependencies, so the package reference is the whole installation.

The package ships as a binary, without source or XML documentation. Author against the EvalApp namespace and let IntelliSense on the public types be your reference.

The fluent builder and the AddStep<TStep>() and AddBranch<TStep>() step-construction paths are safe to trim and to compile ahead of time. The tuner's JSON file persistence and a couple of internal reflection caches are not fully trim-clean, so leave WithTuning off if you publish trimmed and that matters to you.

##### One namespace

Everything you need lives in the root EvalApp namespace: Eval, IAppBuilder, ResourceKind, Tunable, PipelineResult<T>, ICompiledPipeline<T>, the step base classes and licensing. The engine underneath lives in a separate EvalAppEngine namespace that is not part of the supported public surface. If something you need is not reachable from EvalApp, that is a gap to report, not a reason to reach into the engine.

##### Your first pipeline

The quick start on the overview page builds a three-step order pipeline. Four things in it carry through everything below.

- AddStep: Takes a name and a lambda, an async lambda, an IStep<T> instance or a PureStep<T> or AsyncStep<T> subclass.
- Records and with: Each step returns a new value. That is what makes a parallel ForEach safe without locks: no step can see another step's unfinished state.
- Run, then Build: Run(out pipeline) hands you the compiled, reusable pipeline, and Build finalizes the whole app. Build once at startup and call RunAsync many times. Rebuilding per request throws away everything the tuner has learned.
- Results as a union: PipelineResult<T> is Success, Failure or Skipped. Pattern-match it, or use GetData(), IsSuccess, IsFailure and IsSkipped when you only need the value.

##### Design before you build

The biggest lever on whether a pipeline reads cleanly is answering these questions before touching the builder. Each answer constrains the next.

- 1. What is the unit of work?: One sentence: one order, one invoice, one request, one batch.
- 2. What does it start with, carry and produce?: List every piece of information that exists at any point and encode it as a record. A non-nullable field is a required input, a nullable one is an output that appears once its step runs, and a bool is control (loop, branch, skip). If you cannot describe the whole lifecycle by reading the fields, the design is not finished.
- 3. What resource does each operation touch?: Classify each operation as Network, DiskIO, Cpu, Database, a custom ResourceKind.Of("name"), or none. This decides which operations need a gate.
- 4. What runs per item in parallel?: Independent items in a collection, which must not read each other's unfinished state, are ForEach boundaries.
- 5. What conditional branches exist?: For every If and Else, the condition, what each side does, and whether both write the same fields.
- 6. What must be rolled back on failure?: Walk the steps asking what has happened outside the process by the time each completes: money moved, mail sent, a record written. Only external effects need compensation.
- 7. Wire it together: Only now write the fluent declaration. If it does not read like a plain description of the process, the data model needs more work, not more code.

A single-item pipeline with no branches and no external effects skips straight to a flat sequence of steps. That means the problem was simple, not that the method failed.

##### Steps: pure, async and side-effecting

PureStep<T> is a synchronous transform with no side effects, and AsyncStep<T> is the same for work that waits on a network, a disk or a database. A step whose job is a side effect (a database write, a published event, an email) derives from SideEffectStep<T> and declares the ResourceKind it touches.

A SideEffectStep<T> cannot be added with the plain AddStep(name, instance) overload, which fails to compile. Add it with AddStep<TStep>(), which gates it on its declared resource, or with AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) when it needs a constructor-injected dependency. The resource has to be registered on the app first, with WithResource. If you would rather gate explicitly, write the side effect as an async lambda inside a Gate and the gate supplies the resource. Either way there is no path to an ungated side effect.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("StepKinds")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Network)   // a side-effect step is gated on its declared resource
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep("Tax", new ApplyTaxStep())                  // PureStep<T> instance
            .AddStep("Fetch", new FetchTotalStep())              // AsyncStep<T> instance
            .AddStep<SendConfirmationStep>("SendConfirmation")   // SideEffectStep<T>: AddStep<TStep>() only
            .AddStep<PublishEventStep>("Publish", () => new PublishEventStep(new InMemoryBus()))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 100m));
var data = result.GetData();
Console.WriteLine($"{data.Status}: total {data.Total}, tax {data.Tax}");

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New", decimal Tax = 0m);

public sealed class ApplyTaxStep : PureStep<OrderData>
{
    public override OrderData Execute(OrderData data) => data with { Tax = data.Total * 0.08m };
}

public sealed class FetchTotalStep : AsyncStep<OrderData>
{
    public override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Task.Yield();                       // real code: await the actual I/O here
        return data with { Total = data.Total + 1m };
    }
}

public sealed class SendConfirmationStep : SideEffectStep<OrderData>
{
    public override ResourceKind? ResourceKind => EvalApp.ResourceKind.Network;
    public override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Task.Yield();
        return data with { Status = "Confirmed" };
    }
}

public interface IOrderEventBus { ValueTask PublishAsync(string evt, CancellationToken ct); }
public sealed class InMemoryBus : IOrderEventBus
{
    public ValueTask PublishAsync(string evt, CancellationToken ct) => ValueTask.CompletedTask;
}

// A constructor-injected dependency: AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) builds it without a parameterless constructor.
public sealed class PublishEventStep(IOrderEventBus bus) : CrossDomainStep<OrderData, IOrderEventBus>(bus)
{
    public override ResourceKind? ResourceKind => EvalApp.ResourceKind.Network;
    public override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Shared.PublishAsync("OrderPlaced", ct);
        return data with { Status = "Published" };
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
Published: total 101, tax 8.00
```

##### Context-aware steps

When a step needs data that is constant for a whole app run (a configuration, a connection factory) or for a whole domain (a tenant, a region), subclass GlobalContext or DomainContext instead of threading it through every record. The context is populated on the step before it runs.

- Add with AddStep<TStep>(): ContextPureStep and ContextSideEffectStep do not implement the plain IStep<T> that the instance overload expects, so AddStep(name, instance) does not compile for them.
- No StepContext parameter: The public base classes never take one. A type of that name belongs to the internal engine and does not compile against the published package.
- Exceptions become results: Context steps catch their own exceptions and report a Failure, unlike the plain step kinds, which let the exception reach the pipeline.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Context")
    .WithContext(new AppGlobal { Prefix = "ORD" })
    .DefineDomain("Orders", new OrderDomain { Region = "US" })
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep<TagWithRegionStep>("TagRegion")   // context steps are added with AddStep<TStep>() only
            .AddStep<NotifyStep>("Notify")
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");
public sealed class AppGlobal : GlobalContext { public string Prefix { get; init; } = ""; }
public sealed class OrderDomain : DomainContext { public string Region { get; init; } = ""; }

public sealed class TagWithRegionStep : ContextPureStep<AppGlobal, OrderDomain, OrderData>
{
    protected override ValueTask<OrderData> TransformAsync(
        OrderData data, AppGlobal global, OrderDomain domain, CancellationToken ct)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = $"{global.Prefix}:{domain.Region}" });
}

public sealed class NotifyStep : ContextSideEffectStep<AppGlobal, OrderDomain, OrderData>
{
    protected override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(
        OrderData data, AppGlobal global, OrderDomain domain, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Task.Yield();   // real code: the actual notification I/O
        return data with { Status = data.Status + ":Notified" };
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
ORD:US:Notified
```

##### Gates and resource kinds

A Gate declares that everything inside it contends for a named, shared resource. The built-in kinds are Network, DiskIO, Cpu and Database, and ResourceKind.Of("name") defines a pool of your own. Declare a resource's bounds at the app level with WithResource, then gate any block of steps against it.

Without tuning, a gate holds at its declared default. With tuning on, the tuner moves it inside the declared minimum and maximum.

- Tunable.Between(min, max, default): Explicit bounds.
- Tunable.FixedAt(value): Minimum, maximum and default are the same, so there is nothing to tune.
- Tunable.ForCpu(): Scales with the number of processors.
- Tunable.ForItems(): A bound for per-item fan-out, which the tuner can move.
- Tunable.ModelOps(): Fixed at 1, for exclusive access such as GPU training.
- Tunable.DiskIo() and Tunable.Network(): Starting points for those two resource kinds.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Gate")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Database, Tunable.Between(1, 8, 2))
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Of("report-engine"), maxConcurrency: 1)
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .Gate(ResourceKind.Database, onWaiting: null, configure: g => g
                .AddStep("CheckInventory", d => d with { Status = "Checked" }))
            .Gate("CustomPool", Tunable.FixedAt(1),
                onWaiting: null,
                configure: g => g.AddStep("RunReport", d => d with { Status = "Reported" }))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");
```

Output:

```text
Reported
```

##### Parallel collections: ForEach

ForEach runs an independent pipeline over each item of a collection and merges the results back in source order. select extracts the collection, merge combines the results into the parent, and configure builds the per-item pipeline. Parallelism can be a plain number, a function re-read on each run, or a Tunable that the tuner can move.

A ForEach with fewer items than its minimum for parallel work runs inline on the calling thread, whatever the bound says, and the same is true when adaptive dispatch has learned that the items are cheap. The bound caps a fan-out; it never forces one. maxParallelism of 1 is always strictly sequential. Report() shows which path each ForEach took.

- CollectAndThrow: The default. Every item runs and, if any failed, the result is a Failure carrying every exception.
- FailFast: Remaining items are cancelled as soon as one fails.
- ContinueOnError: Failed items are dropped and the result is a Success with the survivors.

For a tight, pure-CPU loop over many cheap rows, repeated many times, use ChunkedWork instead. It fans out in chunks with scratch space allocated once per chunk, which is the right cost model when a per-item pipeline would dominate the work.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

var progress = 0;

Eval.App("ForEach")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<LineItemsData>("CalcLineTotals")
            .ForEach(
                select: d => d.Items,
                merge: (d, items) => d with { Items = items.ToList() },
                collectionName: "Items",
                parallelism: Tunable.ForItems(),
                configure: sub => sub
                    .OnItemCompleted((item, result) => Interlocked.Increment(ref progress))
                    .AddStep("Calc", (LineItem i) => i with { LineTotal = i.Price * i.Quantity }))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<LineItemsData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var items = Enumerable.Range(1, 12).Select(n => new LineItem($"item-{n}", n, 2.5m)).ToList();
var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new LineItemsData(items));
var total = result.GetData().Items.Sum(i => i.LineTotal);
Console.WriteLine($"items: {result.GetData().Items.Count}, progress callbacks: {progress}, total: {total}");

public sealed record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal Price, decimal LineTotal = 0m);
public sealed record LineItemsData(List<LineItem> Items);
```

Output:

```text
items: 12, progress callbacks: 12, total: 195.0
```

##### Conditional and parallel branches

If takes a condition and builder actions for the then and else sides. Without an else and with a false condition the step reports Skipped. Classify is a first-match-wins cascade that names the pattern instead of repeating near-identical If blocks.

AddParallelGroup runs a fixed set of branches at once, as opposed to ForEach, which runs one pipeline per item. Branches that write different fields merge cleanly by default. When two branches might write the same field and that should be a conflict, pass an IMergeStrategy<T>.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Branches")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .If(d => d.Total > 100,
                then: b => b.AddStep("VipDiscount", d => d with { Total = d.Total * 0.8m, Status = "VIP" }),
                @else: b => b.AddStep("StandardProcess", d => d with { Status = "Standard" }))
            .AddParallelGroup(
                pg => pg
                    .AddBranch("CalcTax", d => d with { Tax = d.Total * 0.08m })
                    .AddBranch<CalcShippingBranch>("CalcShipping")
                    .AddBranch("CalcHandling", new CalcHandlingFeeStep()),
                mergeStrategy: new SumNumericFieldsMerge())
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

foreach (var total in new[] { 50m, 200m })
{
    var d = (await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", total))).GetData();
    Console.WriteLine($"{d.Status}: total {d.Total}, tax {d.Tax}, shipping {d.Shipping}, handling {d.Handling}");
}

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New",
    decimal Tax = 0m, decimal Shipping = 0m, decimal Handling = 0m);

public sealed class CalcShippingBranch : PureStep<OrderData>
{
    public override OrderData Execute(OrderData data) => data with { Shipping = 9.99m };
}

public sealed class CalcHandlingFeeStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Handling = 1.5m });
}

public sealed class SumNumericFieldsMerge : IMergeStrategy<OrderData>
{
    public OrderData Merge(OrderData original, IReadOnlyList<OrderData> results)
        => original with
        {
            Tax      = results.Max(r => r.Tax),
            Shipping = results.Max(r => r.Shipping),
            Handling = results.Max(r => r.Handling),
        };
}
```

Output:

```text
Standard: total 50, tax 4.00, shipping 9.99, handling 1.5
VIP: total 160.0, tax 12.800, shipping 9.99, handling 1.5
```

##### Sagas: compensation on failure

A saga chains steps that each declare an undo. If a later step fails, every earlier compensation runs in reverse order. BeginSaga and EndSaga bracket the block, and the compiler refuses a pipeline whose saga is left open.

- BestEffort: The default. Every compensation runs even if one of them throws.
- AbortOnFirst: Stop compensating at the first compensation that fails.
- SwallowErrors: Run every compensation and swallow any exception from them.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Saga")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Database, Tunable.FixedAt(2))
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .BeginSaga(CompensationPolicy.BestEffort)
                .AddStepWithCompensation(
                    "ReserveInventory",
                    forward:    d => d with { Status = "Reserved" },
                    compensate: d => { Console.WriteLine("compensate: release the inventory"); return d with { Status = "Unreserved" }; })
                .AddGate(
                    ResourceKind.Database,
                    onWaiting: null,
                    configure: g => g.AddStep("WriteLedger", d => d with { Total = d.Total }),
                    compensate: new RevertLedgerStep())
                .AddStep(
                    "ChargePayment",
                    d => d.Total > 1_000_000m
                        ? throw new InvalidOperationException("Payment declined")
                        : d with { Status = "Charged" })
            .EndSaga()
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var ok = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Ivy", 10m));
var failed = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Jin", 2_000_000m));
Console.WriteLine($"ok: {ok.IsSuccess}, status {ok.GetData().Status}");
Console.WriteLine($"failed: {failed.IsFailure}, status after compensation {failed.GetData().Status}");

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

public sealed class RevertLedgerStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("compensate: revert the ledger entry");
        return ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = "LedgerReverted" });
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
compensate: revert the ledger entry
compensate: release the inventory
ok: True, status Charged
failed: True, status after compensation New
```

##### Middleware

IStepMiddleware<T> wraps each named step individually, for timing, retry, audit or per-step tracing. No middleware ships ready-made; it is a seam you implement. To wrap the steps of a ForEach item pipeline, register an IStepMiddleware for the item type on that sub-builder.

An exception thrown by a step comes back as a Failure. An exception thrown by middleware outside the call to next is thrown from RunAsync on a top-level pipeline, and is a Failure only when the pipeline is nested in another. A ForEach whose item pipeline is a single synchronous step normally runs as one fused loop, and attaching middleware turns that fast path off.

##### Dependency injection

AddStep<TStep>(name) and AddBranch<TStep>(name) resolve the step through an IStepFactory. The default creates it with a public parameterless constructor. ServiceProviderStepFactory asks your container first and falls back to that for anything not registered.

The compiler enforces the new() constraint whichever factory you register, so a type needs a literal parameterless constructor even if the container always supplies the real one. The factory path is for plain IStep<T> implementers. A side-effect step that needs a constructor-injected dependency uses AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) instead.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

// Any real IServiceProvider works; this minimal one keeps the sample dependency-free.
var services = new SimpleServiceProvider();
services.Register(typeof(ValidateOrderStep), new ValidateOrderStep("DI-resolved"));

Eval.App("Di")
    .WithStepFactory(new ServiceProviderStepFactory(services))
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep<ValidateOrderStep>("Validate")     // resolved from the container, not Activator
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

public sealed class ValidateOrderStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    private readonly string _tag;
    // AddStep<TStep>() needs a literal parameterless constructor; the tagged one is what the container supplies.
    public ValidateOrderStep() : this("default") { }
    public ValidateOrderStep(string tag) => _tag = tag;
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = _tag });
}

public sealed class SimpleServiceProvider : IServiceProvider
{
    private readonly Dictionary<Type, object> _services = new();
    public void Register(Type type, object instance) => _services[type] = instance;
    public object? GetService(Type serviceType) => _services.TryGetValue(serviceType, out var s) ? s : null;
}
```

Output:

```text
DI-resolved
```

##### Pipelines that run pipelines

A compiled pipeline is a value. A step can run another pipeline or itself, and a context can hold a registry of them, so an outer schedule loop drives an inner per-batch pipeline, or a pipeline recurses through a tree, without a hand-written loop around RunAsync. A loop of that kind is invisible to gates and to the tuner; this is how it becomes visible.

PipelineRef<T> forward-declares a pipeline before it is built, PipelineTrace tells same-named steps apart across levels, and a recursion that runs away fails cleanly with PipelineRecursionException instead of overflowing the stack.

##### Exclusive resources

Some things are not thread-safe: a GPU context, a native handle, a file with one writer. Declare an ExclusiveResource once and guard a scope, or named parallel branches, with Exclusive. A second concurrent entry fails loudly with ExclusiveViolationException, or queues if you choose that policy. The guard is re-entrant for recursion, and forks inside a held scope exclude each other instead of silently inheriting it.

##### One-thread hosts

Fanning out only pays when there is a second thread to fan out to. EvalApp detects a single-thread host once, at startup: a browser running Blazor WebAssembly, a process with one processor or one allowed CPU, or a host you declare with ExecutionHost.OverrideSingleThreaded or WithSingleThread. In that mode ForEach, parallel groups and ChunkedWork run inline on the caller, and long runs hand the thread back to the host every few milliseconds (ExecutionHost.YieldBudget) so a page or UI stays responsive. The cancellation token is checked at each yield.

A single very long synchronous step cannot be sliced. Split it into smaller steps or items. Inside a UI, use ChunkedWork.ForAsync and ChunkedWork.RunAsync, which work in time slices. On a multi-core host none of this is active and nothing is added to the fast path.

##### Licensing

No feature in EvalApp is gated behind a tier or a licence key. Every pipeline shape on this page runs at its full declared concurrency whether or not you pass a key, the tuner attaches whenever you call WithTuning, and Build(null) behaves exactly like Build(key).

The licence check exists so that every Evaluated Applications package validates a key the same way. LicenseValidator.ForEvalApp().Check(key) returns Unlicensed or Licensed and never throws, and CheckPeriodic(key, interval) is cheap enough for a hot loop. Verification is entirely offline, with ECDsa P-256, and makes no network call.

EvalApp is proprietary software under a commercial licence. Evaluation and non-commercial development are licensed without a key; commercial, production or revenue-generating use needs a separate licence.

##### Tuning and inspecting

Two opt-in modes. WithTuning is reactive: it rediscovers the operating point on each start, which suits a long-running, stable, single-instance service. WithBayesianTuning is predictive: a performance model persists across restarts, which suits frequent restarts and many instances. Both take an optional store path and share one phase machine, so switching between them does not reset what was learned.

The defaults come from a simulation harness and are what WithTuning uses out of the box. To override them, load your own JSON file with WithTunerSettings(path); the file is read when you call it, and a missing or invalid path throws at that point.

ICompiledPipeline<T> is opaque on purpose: a name and RunAsync. The read-only window on a plan is pipeline.Report(), which lists the plan's nodes and, for each ForEach, how many calls ran inline and how many fanned out. ExecutionHost.Yields counts the yields a process has taken.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

var store = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "evalapp-tuning-sample.json");

Eval.App("Tuned")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Network, Tunable.Between(1, 8, 2))
    .WithTuning(storePath: store)
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<Batch>("Fetch")
            .ForEach(
                select: b => b.Items,
                merge: (b, items) => b with { Items = items.ToList() },
                collectionName: "Items",
                configure: sub => sub
                    .Gate(ResourceKind.Network, onWaiting: null, configure: g => g
                        .AddStep("Download", async (int i, CancellationToken ct) => { await Task.Delay(5, ct); return i + 1; })))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<Batch> pipeline)
    .Build();

for (var run = 0; run < 5; run++)
    await pipeline.RunAsync(new Batch(Enumerable.Range(0, 16).ToList()));

// A read-only window on the compiled plan: each ForEach node counts its calls (and, in Inline and FanOut, how they ran).
foreach (var node in pipeline.Report().Of("ForEach"))
    Console.WriteLine($"{node.Label}: {node.Calls} calls");

File.Delete(store);

public sealed record Batch(List<int> Items);
```

Output:

```text
Items: 5 calls
```

##### Anti-patterns to avoid

The tuner and the gates can only account for work they can see. Anything that happens outside the declared pipeline is invisible to both.

- Task.WhenAll in a step: Use a declared ForEach instead.
- A background Task kept on the record: It races the pipeline, ungated.
- Async work around RunAsync: Work before or after the call, outside the pipeline, is unthrottled and untuned.
- A shared collection written from a ForEach item: It is not thread-safe. Let each item own its result and collect results in merge.
- Mutating the record: Use with. Mutation breaks the guarantee that makes parallel ForEach safe without locks.
- State in step instance fields: Steps are reused by every concurrent run. Per-run state belongs on the record.
- Rebuilding the pipeline per request: It discards everything the tuner has learned. Build once, run many times.
- Blocking calls in a synchronous step: Use the async overload, and pass the cancellation token to every awaited call.
- A hand-written loop or recursion around RunAsync: The loop is invisible to gates and the tuner. Layer and recurse through context instead.
- Guarding a non-thread-safe singleton with a comment: Use an ExclusiveResource.

##### Extension seams

Beyond the fluent API and the step base classes, four extension points are public: GlobalContext and DomainContext (subclass them for WithContext and DefineDomain), IMergeStrategy<T> (custom conflict handling for AddParallelGroup) and IPressureResource (a soft, non-blocking budget signal for Pressure and WithPressure). Everything else is internal to the engine.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### HoloDb: an embedded SQL database for .NET

An embedded SQL database that learns from the queries it serves and keeps only what pays. Every answer is exact, with ACID and no index to design.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb, release 9.0.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client, release 1.5.3: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol, release 1.1.3: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol`
- Builds on: EvalApp, Phasor
- Used by: Prose, HoloGenome
- Tools: Umbrarium, preset demo, The Analyst, Prose

Ask the same question twice and the second time reads almost nothing.

An embedded SQL database for .NET that learns from the queries it serves and keeps only what pays. Every SQL statement is answered exactly, with ACID and no index to design.

- 8.5 to 10 times: fewer blocks read by the next sweep after single-row updates and deletes, because learned records are corrected by the exact difference: 6 blocks against 60 and 51, on 1,000,000 rows
- 61 times: fewer blocks read after consolidation moves the rows: 6 blocks against 366
- 21 to 24 times: fewer page pins when the ledger prices an index by its measured upkeep: 49,306 to 54,106 pins against 1,158,839 over 1,200 delete or update pairs, with 0 blocks read per count
- 0 of 46: recoveries after a kill or a power cut ended in a state between the table before and the table after the interrupted write: 37 to before, 9 to after

HoloDb is an embedded SQL database for .NET. You create tables and write SQL. Tables are typed columns, in memory or on disk. The answer to every SQL statement is exact. NEAREST ranks exactly on small tables and approximately above a size threshold. The engine watches the workload it serves and builds only the structures that repeated queries have paid for. It drops them when the workload moves on or when a write would make them cost more than they save.

One copy of the data answers three kinds of question: a lookup by key in ordinary SQL, similarity search with NEAREST, and exact aggregates that read a maintained total instead of scanning. Everything the engine builds is derived from the columns, so losing a derived structure costs time and never data.

Three terms recur on these pages. A block is a run of rows stored together. A page is 8 KB of file. A pin is one page read through the buffer pool, and counts of pins stand in for time.

Why use it:
- Learned records that stay right when rows change. For a filter you ask for often, the engine writes a card for each block of rows: how many rows match, and the exact sums of the columns you total. The next time you ask, it reads the cards and opens only a block whose card a write has touched. When an UPDATE or DELETE changes rows, or consolidation moves them, the cards are corrected by the exact difference. Each card carries its own checksum lanes and is checked when it is read and when the database opens, so a wrong card is dropped and relearned and never changes an answer.
- A ski-rental ledger decides what to build and what to drop. Renting skis is cheap for one weekend and buying wins after enough weekends. The engine keeps that ledger for every structure. Each scan that a structure would have saved is rent. The structure is built when the rent paid has reached the cost of building it, and dropped when the cost of keeping it up through writes exceeds what it saves. The cost of keeping a structure up is the time its delta path really takes on this machine, measured per write and averaged.
- Gather, regroup and placement lay rows out by what reads waste. If the rows a filter wants are scattered over the whole table, every repeat reads many blocks to find a few rows. The engine measures that waste, in time, for each learned filter. Gather moves matching rows next to each other when the time saved by repeats is larger than the cost of the move. Regroup rewrites the whole layout once, when gather alone cannot reach it. Placement puts a newly written row in a block the repeated filters already read. A repeat that the stored counts and sums already answer reads nothing, so it pays no rent and nothing is moved.
- A paged store with a logical block map. Every page has a logical number, and a map takes that number to a place in the file. The map changes only inside a committed log batch, so a moved or rewritten page never leaves the file half-changed, and a shrunk table keeps its freed pages and refills them. A page that fails its checksum is an error that names the page, never a changed answer.
- ACID with crash-tested recovery. The write-ahead log holds signed page deltas in a ring file whose size follows the largest recent batch, with group commit. A failed statement inside a transaction undoes only itself. A transaction larger than the buffer pool spills to a scratch file, and a rollback or a power cut leaves the table as it was. Each commit is kept as a signed record within a retention budget.
- Real SQL NULL on paged tables. Declare a column NULL and it holds true nulls with three-valued logic, on paged tables as well as in memory. COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip nulls, GROUP BY makes one null group, and a join never matches one. Null counts are maintained. A point read of one row on a wide nullable table takes about 110 page pins at 100,000, 300,000 and 1,000,000 rows.

Capabilities:
- SQL. CREATE TABLE [IF NOT EXISTS], ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, CREATE INDEX (sorted, summary, keyed; automatic indexes need no declaration), DROP INDEX, SHOW INDEXES, SHOW SUMMARIES, SET summaries and SET indexes, EXPLAIN, INSERT (with ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE), UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT with DISTINCT, aggregates, COUNT(DISTINCT), INNER JOIN, WHERE (AND, OR, NOT, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL, IN (SELECT ...)), GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, NEAREST, and BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK.
- Exact. INT sums are 128-bit running totals and throw only past 64 bits. Empty selections give NULL for SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, and 0 for COUNT.
- Learns by use. Summaries, sorted and keyed indexes, a tree of exact sums, learned block records with exact partial sums, learned routes, zones that skip blocks, top-k by zones, gather and placement. One budget covers them all and is a hard cap. EXPLAIN says which structure answered a statement, or why none did.
- Look back. AS OF n and Seal(table, asOf: n) on paged tables.
- Analytic SQL. Narrow column types, dictionary-coded text, CASE, CAST, EXTRACT, DATE_TRUNC, REGEXP_REPLACE, positional GROUP BY and ORDER BY, and COUNT(DISTINCT) on large cardinalities.
- Change feeds. ApplyChanges applies a batch of upserts and deletes atomically. KeyDigest compares two key sets in modulus numbers. Seal fingerprints a table so shards add and replicas compare.
- Aggregate plane (optional). An exact derived summary of small-domain columns, served through Phasor's Pleroma stores, with PleromaVerify to check it against the columns.
- Metering. MeteredDatabase reports the rows and bytes each query read.
- Integration. services.AddHoloDb() for dependency injection, and an EvalApp context for pipelines.

Quick start:

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, age INT, name TEXT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 30, 'Ada')");

var result = await db.ExecuteAsync("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age >= 18");
foreach (var row in result.Rows) Console.WriteLine(row["name"]);
// Ada
```

Output:

```text
Ada
```

Limits:
- Scale: the correctness suites run to 3,000,000 rows in both pipeline modes. Larger tables work, and the benchmark runs to 100,000,000 rows, but the lifecycle and crash guarantees are tested at 3,000,000.
- Writers: one. Reads run in parallel and lock-free for simple selects; writes, DDL and transactions take one lock at a time.
- Joins: INNER JOIN only. A paged table takes one join per statement; in-memory tables take several. A join on a paged table with NULL columns is refused by name.
- SQL not offered: UNION, window functions, subqueries other than IN (SELECT ...), table aliases, DROP COLUMN and column rename. UPDATE ... SET takes a literal on its right side.
- NEAREST: does not combine with GROUP BY or with a join on a nullable table. It ranks exactly on small tables and approximately above a size threshold.
- Keys and types: one primary key per table, INT or TEXT. Types are INT, TEXT and REAL, with narrow integer, date, timestamp and fixed-width text types on analytic tables.
- In-memory only: ApplyChanges and the upsert form run on in-memory tables. A paged table refuses them.
- Row order: without ORDER BY, the order of rows is unspecified and can change after a DELETE or a write that moves a row.
- Structures: they help repeated work. A filter whose matching rows are spread evenly over every block gains nothing from learned records. The first lookup of a value no earlier read has seen is a scan, except a text value absent from the column or a number outside its range, which read no block. Moving scattered rows costs about 200 microseconds per row, so a scattered filter pays that back after about 100 uses.
- Older data: paged tables written by older formats, older write-ahead logs, and a text-format database opened as paged all throw a named error that says to export the rows and load them into a new database. There is no in-place upgrade.
- History: AS OF works on paged tables and reads sequences the history still holds. A sequence below the floor, inside a retained segment, or on an in-memory table is refused by name, as is a join under it.

#### HoloDb docs: tables, SQL, transactions (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/docs/)

The practical guide: put data in, get answers out. The two programs on this page are the complete code, with the output they print.

##### Install and first query

Add the package from NuGet with dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb. You create tables and write SQL. Tables are typed columns, in memory or on disk.

A WalPath in the options makes the database durable. For a database whose tables can be larger than memory, set both WalPath and Paged = true. Paged = true without a WalPath throws.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, age INT, name TEXT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 30, 'Ada')");

var result = await db.ExecuteAsync("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age >= 18");
foreach (var row in result.Rows) Console.WriteLine(row["name"]);
// Ada
```

Output:

```text
Ada
```

##### The SQL dialect

The answer to every SQL statement is exact. Types are INT, TEXT and REAL, with narrow integer, date, timestamp and fixed-width text types on analytic tables. A table has one primary key, INT or TEXT.

- Statements: CREATE TABLE [IF NOT EXISTS], ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, CREATE INDEX, DROP INDEX, SHOW INDEXES, SHOW SUMMARIES, SET summaries, SET indexes, EXPLAIN, INSERT (with ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE), UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT, and BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
- SELECT: DISTINCT, aggregates, COUNT(DISTINCT), INNER JOIN, WHERE with AND, OR, NOT, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL and IN (SELECT ...), GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT and NEAREST.
- Joins: INNER JOIN only. A paged table takes one join per statement; in-memory tables take several. A join on a paged table with NULL columns is refused by name.
- Exact sums: INT sums are 128-bit running totals and throw only past 64 bits. Empty selections give NULL for SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, and 0 for COUNT.
- Analytic SQL: Narrow column types, dictionary-coded text, CASE, CAST, EXTRACT, DATE_TRUNC, REGEXP_REPLACE, positional GROUP BY and ORDER BY, and COUNT(DISTINCT) on large cardinalities.
- Not offered: UNION, window functions, subqueries other than IN (SELECT ...), table aliases, DROP COLUMN and column rename. UPDATE ... SET takes a literal on its right side.
- Row order: Without ORDER BY, the order of rows is unspecified and can change after a DELETE or a write that moves a row.

##### Structures that build themselves

The engine watches the workload it serves and builds only the structures that repeated queries have paid for: summaries, sorted and keyed indexes, a tree of exact sums, learned block records with exact partial sums, learned routes, zones that skip blocks, top-k by zones, gather and placement. It drops them when the workload moves on or when a write would make them cost more than they save. One budget covers them all and is a hard cap.

SET indexes and SET summaries choose whether automatic indexes and summaries are built (auto), only declared ones are kept (declared), or none answers a query (off). EXPLAIN says which structure answered a statement, or why none did. The answers are the same in every setting.

##### NULL

Declare a column NULL and it holds true nulls with three-valued logic, on paged tables as well as in memory. A statement that names a nullable column takes an exact path that reads only the columns it names.

COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip nulls, GROUP BY makes one null group, and a join never matches one. Null counts are maintained. A point read of one row on a wide nullable table takes about 110 page pins at 100,000, 300,000 and 1,000,000 rows.

##### Similarity search

NEAREST ranks rows by how closely they match a partial description, with no separate index. It ranks exactly on small tables and approximately above a size threshold. It does not combine with GROUP BY or with a join on a nullable table.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT, price INT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO products VALUES (1,'electronics',100),(2,'electronics',120),(3,'furniture',300)");

var near = db.Execute("SELECT id, category, price, score FROM products NEAREST (category = 'electronics', price = 118) LIMIT 2");
foreach (var row in near.Rows) Console.WriteLine($"id={row["id"]} category={row["category"]} price={row["price"]} score={row["score"]:F3}");
// id=2 category=electronics price=120 score=0.993
// id=1 category=electronics price=100 score=0.988
```

Output:

```text
id=2 category=electronics price=120 score=0.993
id=1 category=electronics price=100 score=0.988
```

##### Transactions and durability

BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK run over a write-ahead log of signed page deltas in a ring file whose size follows the largest recent batch, with group commit: a statement that has returned is on disk. A failed statement inside a transaction undoes only itself.

A transaction larger than the buffer pool spills to a scratch file, and a rollback or a power cut leaves the table as it was. The tests cut the power inside COMMIT and kill the process, and the table that opens is the table before or the table after.

##### AS OF and Seal

Each commit is kept as a signed record within a retention budget, so SELECT ... FROM t AS OF n reads a paged table as it was after commit n for any n the history still holds. Seal(table, asOf: n) gives an order-free fingerprint that replicas can compare.

AS OF works on paged tables. A sequence below the floor, inside a retained segment, or on an in-memory table is refused by name, as is a join under it.

##### Atomic change batches and upsert

ApplyChanges applies a batch of upserts and deletes atomically. KeyDigest compares two key sets in modulus numbers. Seal fingerprints a table so shards add and replicas compare.

INSERT with ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE is the SQL upsert. ApplyChanges and the upsert form run on in-memory tables, and a paged table refuses them.

##### Tables larger than memory

Paged tables read through a buffer pool of 8 KB pages. Every page has a logical number, and a map takes that number to a place in the file. The map changes only inside a committed log batch, so a moved or rewritten page never leaves the file half-changed, and a shrunk table keeps its freed pages and refills them.

Every log block and every data page carries a CRC-32C checksum. A page that fails its checksum is an error that names the page, never a changed answer. Paged tables written by older formats, older write-ahead logs, and a text-format database opened as paged all throw a named error that says to export the rows and load them into a new database. There is no in-place upgrade.

##### The aggregate plane

The plane is optional. It is an exact derived summary of small-domain columns, served through Phasor's Pleroma stores, with PleromaVerify to check it against the columns.

##### Metering and integration

MeteredDatabase reports the rows and bytes each query read.

services.AddHoloDb() registers HoloDb for dependency injection, and an EvalApp context runs it inside pipelines.

##### Over the network

The same engine runs as a server, and a typed client talks to it over TLS with the same surface as the in-process engine.

#### HoloDb over the network: the client and the wire protocol (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/client/)

HoloDb.Client connects your .NET app to a HoloDb server over TCP with mandatory TLS and token authentication. HoloDb.Protocol is the columnar wire protocol between the two.

##### The client

Run SQL queries and bulk-load data with the same API as the embedded, in-process HoloDbService, so you can move from embedded to networked by changing only how you create the handle. Building a data-driven app usually means choosing between speed (embed the database) and scale (run it on its own server), with two APIs that behave differently. The client gives you one code path for both.

Install it with dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client, or pin it in a project file with the version range 1.5.*. It targets .NET 8 and .NET 10 and needs a HoloDb server it can reach over TLS.

- Same API, embedded or networked: Execute, ExecuteAsync, BulkLoadAsync, GetStatsAsync and PingAsync have the same surface whether you talk to the in-process service or a remote server.
- Columnar over the wire: Results are typed column arrays that match the in-process engine's QueryResult. There is no row buffering and no JSON serialization.
- Secure by default: TLS is on. Trust a self-signed server by pinning its certificate thumbprint, or skip it in development only.
- Resilience when you opt in: Exponential backoff with full jitter, a circuit breaker and a per-operation deadline budget across retries.
- SQL NULL: A NULL cell arrives as DBNull.Value, and IsNull(row, col) tells you which cells are NULL.
- Built for concurrency: One client per concurrent worker, or pool clients up front with HoloDbClientPool.

##### Connect and query

These examples are compiled against the published package. Running them needs a HoloDb server.

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Connect to a server (compile-checked here: running it needs a HoloDb server)
var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("db.example.com", 5433);
try
{
    // The same surface as the in-process HoloDbService; a NULL value is DBNull.Value
    var result = await client.ExecuteAsync("SELECT id, value FROM data LIMIT 10");
    foreach (var row in result.Rows)
        Console.WriteLine($"id={row["id"]}, value={row["value"]}");
}
finally
{
    await client.DisposeAsync();
}
```

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Wraps the client with exponential backoff and a circuit breaker (compile-checked)
var resilient = await ResilientHoloDbClient.ConnectAsync(
    "db.example.com", 5433,
    retryDelay: TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200),
    maxAttempts: 3,
    breakerFailureThreshold: 5);

// Retries transport failures; SQL and authentication errors are not retried
var result = await resilient.ExecuteAsync("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM data");
Console.WriteLine(result.RowCount);
```

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Pin the server certificate by thumbprint, for a self-hosted server (compile-checked)
var options = new HoloDbClientOptions
{
    AuthToken = "your-token",
    UseTls = true,
    PinnedThumbprint = "ABC123DEF456",
};
var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("localhost", 5433, options);
await client.DisposeAsync();
```

##### Things to know

- One client is one session: Requests serialize through an internal queue, and concurrent callers share the same TCP connection. Use one client per worker, or a pool.
- No automatic reconnect: A dropped socket raises an exception, and you reconnect explicitly. ResilientHoloDbClient does this for you when you use it.
- Transient and application errors differ: HoloRemoteException (SQL errors, authentication failures) is not retried. The resilient client retries only transport failures such as IOException and SocketException.
- NULL: Write NULL as the literal NULL in the SQL text. Read it with IsNull(row, col) or GetValue(row, col). A result that holds a NULL is row-form, so the typed GetLong and GetText accessors are for columnar results only. Bulk loads are dense arrays and carry no NULL.
- No parameterised Execute: The client takes SQL text. Use HoloDb.Database.Bind(sql, args) to build the text from values.
- Timeouts: ConnectAsync takes a TimeSpan for the connection only. The resilient client adds an operation timeout to every method, a budget across all its retries.

##### The wire protocol

HoloDb.Protocol defines how the server and client communicate. Instead of sending results as JSON or row objects it keeps the columnar shape: a long[], double[] or string[] travels as a typed array. That keeps the engine's columnar advantage intact when data moves between processes. You normally get the package through HoloDb.Client (version range 1.5.*). Depend on it directly, as EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol with the version range 1.1.*, only to implement a server.

The wire format is stable: opcode byte values never change, and field order and types are fixed. Clients and servers from different builds negotiate a version and fail cleanly when incompatible.

- SQL NULL: A NULL cell travels as its own tag and reaches the client as DBNull.Value (QueryResult.IsNull), never as an empty string.
- Length-prefixed TCP framing: Safe message boundaries, with frame size limits and count bounds checks that stop a hostile length prefix from forcing a huge allocation.
- Binary columnar codec: Typed long, double and string arrays in little-endian format. Non-columnar results (joins, GROUP BY) are packed in a compact binary row format.
- Request and response dispatch: Opcodes for Hello (handshake), Exec (SQL), BulkLoad, Stats and Ping.
- Error semantics: Protocol errors (corrupt or malformed bytes) are distinct from query errors (bad SQL, a constraint violation), so a caller knows whether to retry.
- Transport-agnostic: It works over TCP, TLS or any duplex Stream. The protocol provides no encryption: TLS is the transport layer's job, and the authentication token travels in the Hello handshake as UTF-8, so run it over TLS.

A columnar query returns column arrays, not rows. If you expect row-by-row iteration, read the columns by position as above, or use Rows to materialise dictionaries.

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Reading a columnar result without row unpacking (compile-checked here; it needs a server to run)
await using var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("localhost", 5433, new HoloDbClientOptions { AuthToken = "mytoken" });
var result = await client.ExecuteAsync("SELECT id, price FROM prices");

if (result.IsColumnar)
{
    // column 0 is a long, column 1 is a double
    for (int r = 0; r < result.RowCount; r++)
        Console.WriteLine($"ID {result.GetLong(r, 0)}: price {result.GetDouble(r, 1)}");
}
```

```csharp
using HoloDb;
using HoloDb.Protocol;

// A server loop built on the wire protocol (compile-checked here; it needs a connected stream to run)
async Task HandleOneRequest(Stream networkStream, HoloDbService engine, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var payload = await Wire.ReadFrameAsync(networkStream, ct);
    var request = HoloProtocol.DecodeRequest(payload);

    if (request.Op == WireOp.Exec)
    {
        var result = await engine.ExecuteAsync(request.Sql);
        var response = HoloProtocol.Result(result);
        await Wire.WriteFrameAsync(networkStream, response, ct);
    }
}
Console.WriteLine(nameof(HandleOneRequest));
```

### AlgFormer: small language models in one shared wave, for .NET

A population of small holographic language models that talk through a shared wave, in pure managed code.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer, release 3.4.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu, release 1.13.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu`
- Builds on: EvalApp, Phasor
- Used by: Prose
- Tools: Prose

Many small models, one shared wave.

A population of small holographic language models that talk through a shared wave, in pure managed code. They never pass wires to each other. They write to the medium and read the medium.

- 2.99 against 3.38: bits per character: six atoms that each see about a sixth of the text and share the medium, against one atom that reads all of it. The same six atoms without the medium score 4.33
- 3.47 against 3.84: bits per character for two width-32 atoms when the loss reaches the atoms through the notes they wrote, against the same atoms with the writer gradient switched off
- 261 launches: per training step for two, eight and sixteen atoms alike, against 454 for two atoms and 1,672 for eight on the per-atom path (two layers, two passes)
- 26 times: less time to read a 1,984-token prompt with holographic attention

AlgFormer is a .NET library for defining, training and running transformer-style language models, built on the Phasor codec. The atom field is the part that couples models. Several small HoloFormers, with no shared weights, write into one bundle of damped oscillators and listen to each other's notes. The answer you serve is the average of their logits, and you can train on that combined answer. The library also holds the two single-model cores, a softmax core and a holographic core, with a subword tokenizer, a data-parallel trainer, streaming generation with a cache and checkpoints. Everything is plain double arrays with SIMD. No GPU, Python or native runtime is needed, and an optional GPU package runs the same models faster.

Think of a pond with sources and listeners. Each atom is a small HoloFormer. At every position it writes its state into one shared bundle of damped oscillators, like dropping a pebble of its own size and phase into the water. Each atom then listens to the pond with its own note removed, so it hears only the others.

Time lives in the medium itself. Each oscillator advances in phase and decays a little at every step, so recent writes ring loud and old writes fade, and fast bells and slow bells keep different spans of history. Space lives in the medium as well. With holographic locality, every atom has a trainable position and every channel a trainable wavevector. A writer binds a phase set by where it sits, and a reader unwinds the phase set by where it sits, so near atoms add up together and far atoms drift out of step.

In the golden configuration the atoms start on a golden-ratio spiral with golden-angle write phases, so none sits in a privileged place, and the timescales are rotated around the golden ratio from atom to atom, so every atom owns the same mix of fast and slow bells. With holographic locality, or with no locality, the cost grows linearly with the number of atoms and with the length of the text. Dense locality, the default mode when locality is switched on, costs the square of the number of atoms.

Why use it:
- Holographic bundle attention, no softmax. A standard transformer scores every token against every other token with softmax, which is quadratic in the length. HoloFormer binds each key to its value, folds them into one running bundle and unbinds with the query. Reading a prompt grows in step with its length, and serving each further token through Prime and Step costs the same however long the context is.
- Weight-tied depth. One layer's weights are reused for several passes, so depth is a count you choose rather than a parameter bill. The atom field runs the same K passes for every layer of every atom.
- A population coupled by a medium. Standard ensembles average finished answers. Here the atoms exchange information while they compute, through one shared bundle of damped oscillators. With holographic locality or none, the cost grows linearly with their number.
- Trainable geometry. Atom positions, wavevectors, decay times and write phases are learned parameters with exact gradients. Every dense map is a relation bank, so a layer carries S times d parameters rather than d squared.

Capabilities:
- Two comparable single-model cores. AlgFormer (softmax) and HoloFormer (holographic) share a model shape, a training loop, a checkpoint format and a serving API. The atom field builds a population out of HoloFormer models.
- AtomField. Opt-in, Memory coupling: N HoloFormers with no shared weights coupled through one damped-oscillator bundle, each reading the others with its own note removed, serving the mean of the atoms' logits. Training can use per-atom loss or the combined loss (CombinedLoss) on the mean of the logits. Weight-tied passes (Iters) per layer.
- Locality. Trainable atom positions and per-channel wavevectors (MemoryLocality, holographic and dense modes; holographic is linear in the number of atoms, dense is quadratic), with a golden-spiral start (SpiralPositions).
- Diversity options. All off by default: golden rotation of timescales (MemoryTauRotation, GoldenTauRotations), a fast-to-slow scale ladder (MemoryTauScale) and golden-angle write phases (MemoryWritePhaseDeg).
- Molecules. MemoryMoleculeSize groups atoms so each hears its group in one amplitude and the rest in another. It runs on the CPU only.
- Trajectory accessor and checkpoints. TrajectoryAllPositions for viewers, and checkpoints for the whole field (SerializeMemory, LoadMemory).
- Data-parallel training. Through an EvalApp pipeline (PrismTrainer).
- Streaming inference. Prime and Step with an incremental cache, constant work per token for HoloFormer.
- Growth and sizing. In-place model growth, a capacity-law sizing module (HoloShape, including HoloShape.Derive), a built-in subword tokenizer and data-source adapters.
- Preference training. Preference (DPO) training on the CPU HoloFormer.
- ADAM and EVE. An opt-in per-layer Adam gate for HoloFormer, default off.
- Gradient-check oracles. Built-in checks let you verify the training maths instead of assuming it is right.
- Interpretability hooks. AlgFormer.AttentionWeights and HoloFormer.InspectAttention.
- Relay components. MQTT relay components (MqttRelay, MqttJobRelay, JobSource and a peer gossip component) can move batches, or position manifests with no data, between machines. They are separate from the atom field, which has no relay.

Quick start:

```csharp
using PrismFormer;

// Two HoloFormer atoms (width 32, 2 layers, vocabulary 16, context 8), coupled through the shared memory.
var field = AtomField.Create(atoms: 2, dim: 32, layers: 2, vocab: 16, context: 8, seed: 1);
field.Coupling = AtomCoupling.Memory;

// One example is one token window per atom (at most context + 1 tokens, the same length for every atom).
var examples = new List<int[][]> { new[] { new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 }, new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 } } };
double loss = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) loss = field.TrainStepAllPositions(examples, lr: 0.01);

var result = field.InferAllPositions(examples[0]);   // result.Logits is the mean of the atoms' logits
Console.WriteLine($"loss={loss:F3} logits={result.Logits.Length} atoms={result.AtomLogits.Length}");
```

Output:

```text
loss=0.160 logits=16 atoms=2
```

Limits:
- Held-out text: the harness results are scored on 300 held-out windows of their own book text. The six-atom checkpoints are scored on windows of their training text.
- Default: the atom field is opt-in in the library and the studio. A plain HoloFormer is what you get by default.
- Scale: the harness results are small models on one text, two seeds.
- Diversity: the diversity options (golden rotation of timescales, golden-angle write phases) are off by default. In the width-64 four-atom test, rotation raised how much the atoms depend on each other (leave-one-out cost 0.16 to 0.21) without lowering their correlation or improving the score.
- Cost: linear in the number of atoms with holographic locality or no locality. Dense locality is quadratic in the number of atoms.
- Molecules: MemoryMoleculeSize runs on the CPU only. The GPU package ignores it.
- Holographic capacity: a holographic bundle holds a limited number of items cleanly, and HoloShape reports how many for a shape.

#### How HoloFormer works (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer/holoformer/)

Attention that stays fast as the context grows.

HoloFormer folds everything it has read into one running memory per layer. Reading a prompt grows with its length instead of its square, and each new word costs the same however long the context is.

- 26 times: less time to read a 1,984-token prompt with holographic attention
- 50 times: less time for each further token, which stays flat as the context grows
- 663 times: smaller serve cache, constant in the length of the context

HoloFormer is the holographic attention core in AlgFormer. This page explains it in plain terms: how a token is stored, how ideas are combined, how the model thinks longer and how it remembers a whole context in one place. Each idea ends by naming the part of the model it describes.

##### A token is a chord

Give the model a letter, a word or a number and it writes it down as a chord: a particular stack of pure tones played together. Each tone is one channel of a complex-valued vector, and the chord is the whole vector. One word is one chord and another word is another.

How many tones can a chord stack? That is the size of the instrument. A small instrument has few strings, so chords blur into one another and the model cannot tell things apart. A bigger instrument keeps chords crisp and distinct.

- In the model: The tones are the channels, set by dModel when you construct the model. More channels keep meanings distinct.

##### Combining is playing together

The model has essentially one core move. To join two things it plays their chords together, and they merge into a single new chord. That is how a word is tied to its role, or a question to its subject.

Numbers are chords tuned so that playing two of them together adds their values. The chord for 5 played with the chord for 3 decodes as 8. The arithmetic is in the sound itself, so the model does not have to memorise a times table the way an ordinary transformer would. The program below is the Phasor codec that supplies the chords.

```csharp
using Phasor;

// Encode a number and some symbols
double[] five = PhasorCodec.Encode("5");
double[] three = PhasorCodec.Encode("3");
double[] age = PhasorCodec.Encode("age");
double[] name = PhasorCodec.Encode("name");
double[] hello = PhasorCodec.Encode("hello");

// Bind two numbers: adds them on the linear band
double[] fivePlusThree = PhasorCodec.Bind(five, three);
Console.WriteLine($"5 + 3 = {PhasorCodec.DecodeSum(fivePlusThree, max: 10)}");

// Bind each value to a role, bundle the pairs into one record, then unbind a role to read its value back
double[] record = PhasorCodec.Bundle(PhasorCodec.Bind(age, five), PhasorCodec.Bind(name, hello));
double[] ageField = PhasorCodec.Unbind(record, age);
Console.WriteLine($"age field matches 5 better than 3: {PhasorCodec.Correlate(ageField, five) > PhasorCodec.Correlate(ageField, three)}");

// For larger workloads and similarity search, HoloCodec is SIMD and configurable in width
var codec = new HoloCodec(dim: 1024);
double[] encoded = codec.Encode("hello");
Console.WriteLine($"HoloCodec self-similarity is positive: {HoloCodec.Dot(encoded, codec.Encode("hello")) > 0}");
```

Output:

```text
5 + 3 = 8
age field matches 5 better than 3: True
HoloCodec self-similarity is positive: True
```

##### Chord moves

Stacking chords is not enough. The model also has to transform them, steering a question toward its answer. It does this with a small set of learned moves, each of which blends in tones from elsewhere on the instrument.

More moves let it express richer relationships. The moves are spread across the instrument rather than only nudging neighbouring strings, so it can connect distant ideas and not only adjacent notes. At least two are needed: with one move every tone only ever reads itself, and nothing can route between tones.

- In the model: The moves are the shifts of the relation bank, spread by golden-ratio spacing so a few of them cover the whole range. HoloShape.ShiftsFor chooses how many a given context needs.

##### A chain of arrangers

The sound is not shaped all at once. It flows through several stages in a row, and each stage restyles it with its own set of moves before handing it on, the way a melody passes through a chain of arrangers.

- In the model: The stages are the layers. Depth is how many times the sound is reworked.

##### Play it through twice

Thinking, for this model, is replaying. Each stage can play its part again over what it just laid down, and only then hand the sound on. The first pass sketches and the second develops the sketch.

Replaying costs no extra parameters, because the same stage is simply applied again. The model can think harder about a short input by playing it through more times, and a newly added stage can be eased in by letting its replay weight start at zero and ramp up.

- In the model: The repeats are the K weight-tied iterations of each layer (the StackIter family), with a per-layer alpha that ramps a new layer in.

##### One shared sound you tune into

This is where HoloFormer parts company with an ordinary transformer. A transformer makes every position compare itself with every earlier position: a crowded room in which everyone talks to everyone, and the effort grows with the square of the conversation.

HoloFormer folds everything it has heard into one running sound per layer. Each position binds its key to its value and adds the result to the bundle. To recall something, the query is unbound from the bundle: the matching part rings out and the rest averages toward silence, like finding one station on a radio dial.

One bundle holds the whole context, so reading a prompt grows with its length rather than its square, and each new token costs the same however long the context has become. The chart on the overview page measures both cores. The held memory can also be listened to: the inspectors read off what the final query resonated with and decode it to tokens.

- In the model: This is holographic memory: retrieval by resonance instead of every-position-to-every-position comparison. The incremental cache of this core is one running bundle per layer.

##### How much one sound can hold

Many bound pairs summed into one vector crosstalk: each read comes back with a little noise from all the others. A bundle can therefore hold a limited number of items cleanly. HoloShape reports two numbers for a shape. The crosstalk edge is the number of shifts times the width, halved. The clean capacity is the number of tokens that read back at least 90 percent clean, which is about 12 percent of the edge.

Models are sized so that the context sits at a chosen fraction of the edge, and the default is a quarter. At a width of 128, HoloShape derives a context of 2,048 tokens. The crosstalk edge there is 8,192 tokens and 983 tokens read back clean. The constants behind the derived shapes are single measurements, so treat the shape as a starting point.

```csharp
using PrismFormer;

int ctx = 64, dim = 32;
int shifts = HoloShape.ShiftsFor(ctx, dim);                       // the normal way to choose Shifts
bool collides = HoloShape.ShiftsCollide(shifts, dim, golden: true);
Console.WriteLine($"ShiftsFor({ctx},{dim}) = {shifts}, collides = {collides}");
Console.WriteLine($"bind rank {HoloShape.BindRank(shifts, dim)}, reads back clean {HoloShape.CleanCapacity(shifts, dim)}");

// A starting shape from a width alone. Treat it as a place to begin, not a guarantee.
foreach (var width in new[] { 64, 128, 256 })
{
    var s = HoloShape.Derive(width, stackK: 2);
    Console.WriteLine($"Derive({width}): shifts {s.Shifts}, context {s.Context}, layers {s.Layers}");
}
```

Output:

```text
ShiftsFor(64,32) = 16, collides = False
bind rank 256, reads back clean 30
Derive(64): shifts 64, context 512, layers 3
Derive(128): shifts 128, context 2048, layers 6
Derive(256): shifts 256, context 8192, layers 8
```

##### Side by side with an ordinary transformer

An ordinary transformer memorises the music. This one plays it.

##### Try it

The holographic core takes the same constructor as the softmax core. This program trains one, serves it through the incremental cache and reads what its final query resonated with.

```csharp
using PrismFormer;

// The holographic core has the same constructor shape. Swap the type, keep the workflow.
var holo = new HoloFormer(vocab: 16, shifts: 4, layers: 2, maxContext: 6, dModel: 32, frozenPrefix: 0);

var data = new List<(int[] Ctx, int Target)>
{
    (new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, 4),
    (new[] { 2, 3, 4 }, 5),
};
double loss = holo.TrainEpoch(data, batchSize: 2, lr: 5e-2, shuffleSeed: 1);

// Serve with the incremental cache: one running holographic memory per layer, so each token costs the same
// however long the context has become.
var cache = holo.NewCache();
double[] afterPrompt = holo.Prime(cache, new[] { 1, 2, 3 });
double[] afterNext = holo.Step(cache, 4);

// Read the model's mind: the resonance of the final query against every earlier position, and what it retrieved.
var alpha = new double[holo.Layers]; Array.Fill(alpha, 1.0);
int[] toks = { 1, 2, 3 };
double[][] resonance = holo.InspectAttention(toks, K: 2, alpha);
double[] retrieved = holo.InspectRetrieval(toks, K: 2, alpha);
double[] decoded = holo.DecodeFace(retrieved);          // per-token logits for what the query pulled out

Console.WriteLine($"loss={loss:F3} cache length={cache.Length} logits lengths {afterPrompt.Length},{afterNext.Length}");
Console.WriteLine($"resonance rows={resonance.Length}, positions per row={resonance[0].Length}, decoded logits={decoded.Length}");
```

Output:

```text
loss=2.777 cache length=4 logits lengths 16,16
resonance rows=4, positions per row=3, decoded logits=16
```
